analysis.one_liner: Restores and strengthens federal protections against workplace discrimination, adding money damages and longer filing deadlines.
analysis.headline: Both chambers passed the Civil Rights Act of 1990 by wide margins — 65-34 in the Senate and 273-154 on the conference report — but President Bush vetoed it and a Senate override fell one vote short at 66-34.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill rolled back a series of 1989 Supreme Court decisions that had made job discrimination cases much harder to win. It shifted the burden to employers to prove that hiring and promotion rules with unequal effects on women and minorities are genuine business necessities, extended the deadline to file a discrimination charge from 180 days to two years, and — for the first time under the main employment discrimination law — allowed compensatory and punitive damages, with jury trials, for intentional discrimination.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers who face discrimination in hiring, promotion, pay, or firing — especially women, racial and religious minorities, older workers, and people with disabilities. They would get up to two years (instead of 180 days) to file a charge, an employer's burden to justify job requirements that screen out protected groups, money damages and jury trials for intentional discrimination, protection for court-ordered discrimination settlements from outside challenges, and restored rights to sue over race discrimination in making and enforcing contracts.

how_it_helps.text: Shifts the burden of proof in disparate-impact cases: once a worker shows an employment practice (or group of practices) disproportionately screens out people by race, sex, religion, or national origin, the employer must demonstrate the practice is required by business necessity — codifying the Griggs standard and overturning the 1989 Wards Cove decision.

Doubles the time to file a discrimination charge from 180 days to two years, and lets workers challenge discriminatory seniority systems in collective bargaining agreements for as long as those systems keep applying against them.

For the first time allows compensatory damages — and punitive damages where there is malice or reckless indifference — plus a jury trial, for intentional discrimination under Title VII and in disability discrimination cases.
Protects litigated and consent judgments resolving discrimination claims from being challenged by outsiders who had notice and a chance to object, preserving the durability of agreed remedies.
Restores the right to sue over race discrimination in the making, performance, and enforcement of contracts, and adds expert fees and litigation expenses to recoverable attorney's fees.

analysis.who_pays: Employers facing discrimination claims. They would bear the burden of proving that job requirements with unequal effects are business necessities, could owe compensatory and punitive damages and jury awards for intentional discrimination, and would face longer exposure to claims under the two-year filing window and retroactive application to cases pending since mid-1989.

drawbacks.text: Opponents, including President Bush, argued the burden-of-proof changes would pressure employers into hiring and promotion quotas. The bill expressly states it does not require quotas (Section 13), and the House voted 375-45 to instruct conferees to add language saying businesses need not adopt quotas — but the objection drove the veto.

Expanded damages, jury trials, and the ability to attack a whole 'group of employment practices' rather than a single one would raise litigation costs and settlement exposure for employers, including those who never intended to discriminate.

The bill applied retroactively, reaching cases and proceedings pending since as early as May and June 1989, and directed courts to vacate inconsistent orders entered in the interim — reopening matters employers believed were settled.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The gains for workers are concrete: longer filing windows, a fairer burden of proof in disparate-impact cases, and real money damages for intentional discrimination, which previously carried essentially no penalty beyond back pay. The costs fall mainly on employers, in higher litigation expense and liability. The quota argument that carried the veto was contested — the bill expressly disclaims quotas and the final version limited damages and jury trials to intentional-discrimination claims — but the group-of-practices burden-shifting genuinely would have made it harder for employers to defend neutral procedures, and that is the strongest good-faith case against the bill.

outcome.mechanism: President George H.W. Bush vetoed the bill on October 22, 1990, and the Senate's attempt to override fell one vote short of the two-thirds needed, 66-34; the House never voted on an override and the bill died.

narrative.text: The Senate passed the bill 65-34 on July 19, 1990, with all 55 Democrats and 10 Republicans in favor, after invoking cloture on a related amendment 62-38 when Republicans initially delayed action.
The House passed the measure without objection on August 3 by striking the Senate text and inserting its own version (the text of similar H.R. 4000), then requested a conference.

The conference report — adding limits such as confining damages and jury trials to intentional-discrimination claims and capping punitive damages — was agreed to by the Senate 62-34 (53 Democrats, 9 Republicans) and the House 273-154 (239 Democrats, 34 Republicans).

President Bush vetoed the bill on October 22; the Senate override vote on October 24 reached 66-34 — all 55 Democrats plus 11 Republicans — one vote short of the 67 required, and the House never took up an override.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: President Bush and the 34 Senate Republicans who voted to sustain his veto came out ahead: employers avoided the bill's new burden of proof, damage exposure, and retroactive reach, while workers who had gained stronger remedies under both chambers' versions got nothing in that Congress.

for.name: Edward M. Kennedy
for.role: U.S. Senator from Massachusetts; Chairman, Senate Labor and Human Resources Committee
for.what_they_did: Introduced and sponsored the bill, reported it from committee with an amendment, managed Senate floor action, and led the Senate conferees.

for.name: 55 of 55 Senate Democrats
for.what_they_did: Voted unanimously for final passage (65-34) and for the conference report (62-34), and all 55 voted to override the veto.

for.name: 239 of 257 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Provided the votes for the conference report, 239-15, after passing the House version without objection in August.

for.name: Augustus F. Hawkins
for.role: Chairman, House Education and Labor Committee
for.what_they_did: Brought the bill to the House floor, chaired the House conferees, and managed the conference report in the House.

for.name: 10 of 45 Senate Republicans
for.what_they_did: Voted for final passage; 9 also voted for the conference report and 11 voted to override the veto.

against.name: President George H.W. Bush
against.what_they_did: Vetoed the bill on October 22, 1990, calling it a quota bill, and the veto stood when the override fell short.

against.name: 34 of 45 Senate Republicans
against.what_they_did: Voted against cloture, against final passage, and against the override — providing the margin that sustained the veto.

against.name: 139 of 175 House Republicans
against.what_they_did: Voted against the conference report; 169 of 176 had earlier voted for a motion to recommit demanding quota-disclaimer language.

against.name: U.S. Chamber of Commerce and business coalitions
against.what_they_did: Campaigning against the bill as a quota and litigation-expansion measure, in support of the veto position.

sides.party_line_note: Passage votes split sharply by party — the Senate went 55-0 among Democrats versus 10-34 among Republicans, and the House conference vote 239-15 among Democrats versus 34-139 among Republicans — though the House's motion to recommit on quota language passed 375-45 with heavy support from both parties.

industries.industry: Private employers (all businesses covered by Title VII)
industries.note: The bill would have required employers to prove that hiring, testing, and promotion rules with unequal effects are genuine business necessities, and exposed them to compensatory and punitive damages and jury trials for intentional discrimination. Employer groups' central objection — that the changes would pressure them toward quotas — carried the day with the veto, though the bill's text expressly disclaimed quotas.

New damage claims, jury trials, a two-year filing window, and fee awards including expert fees and litigation expenses would have expanded employment discrimination practice. Their gain runs alongside workers', since fees are recovered from losing employers.
They would have faced the same burden-of-proof changes but with a punitive damages cap tied to $150,000 or other monetary relief, whichever is greater — a concession won in the conference report.
